# Regular expression built from HTTP request data (Java)

`qualor:java/regex-injection` · Issue · Severity: Medium · [CWE-1333](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1333.html), [CWE-400](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data used as a regular expression (Jakarta Servlet, Spring MVC, Jakarta REST): the
pattern given to `Pattern.compile` or `Pattern.matches`, or the regex argument of the `String`
methods `matches`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`, `split` and `splitWithDelimiters`. Request data
as the text a constant pattern is applied to, as a replacement text, quoted with `Pattern.quote`,
or compiled with the `Pattern.LITERAL` flag is not reported.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
`java.util.regex` is a backtracking engine: a pattern such as `(a+)+$` can take exponential time on
a short input, so one request can keep a server thread busy for minutes (regular expression denial
of service, ReDoS). A request-chosen pattern can also match far more than the code intends, for
example `.*` in a filter that should match one name.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the search term is compiled as a pattern.

```java
package com.example.search;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class NameController {
    private final List<String> names = List.of("alice", "bob", "carol");

    @GetMapping("/names")
    public List<String> find(@RequestParam String q) {
        Pattern pattern = Pattern.compile(q);
        return names.stream().filter(n -> pattern.matcher(n).find()).toList();
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** the term is quoted, so it matches only itself.

```java
package com.example.search;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class NameController {
    private final List<String> names = List.of("alice", "bob", "carol");

    @GetMapping("/names")
    public List<String> find(@RequestParam String q) {
        Pattern pattern = Pattern.compile(Pattern.quote(q));
        return names.stream().filter(n -> pattern.matcher(n).find()).toList();
    }
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- To search for the text the user typed, quote it: `Pattern.compile(Pattern.quote(q))`, or
  compile it with `Pattern.LITERAL`; to split or replace on it, use `split(Pattern.quote(sep))` or
  `String.replace`, which takes a literal target.
- If users must choose between patterns, pick the pattern from a fixed allow-list (a `Map.of` of
  constant patterns or an enum) by a key from the request.
- Keep request data on the other side: match it against a constant pattern
  (`q.matches("[\\w ]+")`).
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Jakarta Servlet
- Spring MVC
- Jakarta REST (JAX-RS)

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- The `String` methods are checked only on a receiver whose type is visible as `String` (a typed
  variable, parameter or field, or a literal); on a `var` or the result of a call they are missed,
  because other libraries have methods named `matches`, `split` and `replaceAll`.
- Other APIs that take a pattern as text, such as `java.util.Scanner`'s `findInLine`, `hasNext`,
  `next`, `skip` and `useDelimiter`, and regex helpers of other libraries, are not checked.
- A value first checked against a constant pattern (`if (!q.matches("[\\w ]+")) return;`) is
  still reported.
- A handler parameter without an annotation is not a source (the Jakarta REST entity parameter, a
  Spring MVC simple-type parameter), except a Spring `HttpEntity` or `RequestEntity` (the
  request body and headers); enum, `List` or `Optional` parameters still count as request data.
- One method is analysed at a time and conditions are not evaluated: a helper that returns a
  constant, or a switch over a constant, still passes the request data on, and a wrapper class that
  reads the request is not a source. Allow-list lookups are recognised only as `Map.of(...)` of
  constants and as `valueOf` of an enum declared in the same file, but not of an enum nested in
  the file's only class.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/java/regex/regex-injection.java`](../../../rules/java/regex/regex-injection.java) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/java/regex/regex-injection.yml`](../../../rules/java/regex/regex-injection.yml), added in version 2026.10.2.
